12.0.0.en: Abram: a name meaning exalted father or honored father.

12.0.1.en: God's call to Abram came first in Ur of the Chaldees, as we mentioned, but it was delayed because of the attachment of his father Terah to him, who preferred to stay in Haran for about 14 years. Then God renewed the call to Abram a second time, to go out from the place where he was living. This shows God's long-suffering and His love for Abram, the only man in the world who worshipped God, together with Sarai his wife and Lot his nephew, who was attached to him, while the rest of the world worshipped idols. So God made allowance for Abram, who was ashamed to oppose his father and deprived himself of dwelling with God in the new land for no short time; and when God repeated the call to him, he obeyed this time. This call includes the following:

12.0.2.en: 1- From your country: that is, Ur of the Chaldees, or Haran, which lies to its north, so that he might keep away from the worship of idols. Spiritually it signifies leaving the perishable earthly attachments for the sake of God.

12.0.3.en: 2- From your kindred and from your father's house: that is, all his relatives to whom he was attached emotionally, and who represented protection and reassurance to him, because they were bound to the worship of idols and his staying with them would hinder him from worshipping God.

12.0.4.en: 3- To a land that I will show you: God did not specify a place for him to live in; it was enough for him to be with God in any place He chose for him, and this is reliance on God.

12.0.5.en: If you believe in God, do not fear the future or be troubled by any strange thing that comes upon you, but leave God to order your life as He sees fit, for He knows your good better than you do and chooses what is best for you.

12.0.6.en: 4- I will make you a great nation: although Sarai was barren and Abram was 75 years old, God promised him not only offspring, but that his seed would become very numerous and be a great nation. In proportion to a person's obedience to God's commandments, which may seem hard, God gives him an indescribably great blessing and helps him to carry out His commandments, for God is rich and cannot be indebted to anyone.

12.0.7.en: 5- I will bless you and make your name great: Abram would not be an ordinary person but one blessed by God in his health and his possessions, and everyone with him would enjoy his peace; indeed he would be great in the eyes of all around him. This is God's grace to His children who obey Him.

12.0.8.en: 6- You shall be a blessing: not only would he be blessed by God, but a blessing to those around him, so that everyone who clings to him receives a blessing, as Christ promised His children that they would be the light of the world (Mt 5:14).

12.1.0.en: 7- I will bless those who bless you: part of God's blessing to Abram is that everyone who treats him well, praises him and follows his example, God blesses, because Abram is the image of God among the Gentiles, that they may learn from him and God may bless them, just as every Christian is the image of God in the midst of society.

12.1.1.en: 8- I will curse him who curses you: on the other hand, God promises wrath and vengeance on everyone who opposes or wrongs Abram, for He gives him awe in the eyes of all around him, so that they fear to wrong him lest divine wrath fall upon them, and thus the fear of him is in the hearts of all.

12.1.2.en: 9- In you all the families of the earth shall be blessed: Abram becomes a blessing to the whole world, and this is fulfilled in Christ, who comes from his seed and gives salvation to the whole world, to everyone who believes in Him.

12.2.0.en: Abram obeyed God's word in spite of its difficulty. He left the fortified cities, his family and his loved ones to go to an unknown place and live among people he did not know, but he would enjoy God's presence with him, and this surpasses every pleasure in the world; it is paradise on earth. Abram took with him his wife Sarai and Lot his nephew, who loved his uncle and was attached to him, and he took his light belongings such as clothing and tents, and likewise his servants, and moved with God, who led him to the land of Canaan; so he crossed the river Euphrates to enter it.

12.3.0.en: Shechem: it is present-day Nablus, about 41 miles north of Jerusalem and five and a half miles southeast of Samaria. It is a valley, with Mount Ebal extending to its north and Mount Gerizim to its south. Jacob also lived in it and bought a piece of a field in it; Dinah, Jacob's daughter, sinned with Shechem the son of Hamor in it, and Reuben and Simeon, the sons of Jacob, killed the men of the tribe of Shechem; and Joseph was buried in it.

12.3.1.en: The terebinth (oak) of Moreh: a region with many large oak trees, and Moreh means teacher. It seems that a teacher used to sit in this place and people would come to him.

12.3.2.en: The Canaanites: they were distinguished by city life and the building of houses and cities, and they were wicked, immersed in many lusts. Abram arrived at a region called Shechem in the land of Canaan, stayed in it for a time, and then moved to another region called the oak of Moreh (maps 5, 6).

12.4.0.en: God appeared a third time to Abram when he reached the land of Canaan, and declared His promise to give him the land of Canaan in which he dwelt. Abram thanked God and expressed his thanks by building an altar to God there and offering thanksgiving sacrifices to Him. Thus the land of Canaan was blessed for the first time with prayer and worship offered to God instead of the worship of idols, and a sacrifice was offered to God that signifies Christ, who would come in the fullness of time to the land of Canaan to redeem all mankind.

12.4.1.en: Do not leave any place you pass through in your whole life without raising a prayer to God, so that the place is sanctified by prayer, you feel God's presence with you, and He also blesses those who are in it. And if you cannot stand to pray, then at least lift your heart to God, who sees you and rejoices in your prayers.

12.5.0.en: Bethel: it means the house of God, and it lies east of Jerusalem, midway between it and Nablus (Shechem); its old name was Luz.

12.5.1.en: Ai: it means a heap of ruins, and it lies east of Bethel.

12.5.2.en: Abram moved to Bethel and settled to its west, with the city of Ai lying to its east. Thus he moved from Shechem toward the south, and this declares that he was a stranger in the land, moving with his tent from place to place, and he was not influenced by the behavior of the wicked Canaanites around him; rather he cared for his relationship with God, so he built a new altar beside Bethel, offered sacrifices and raised prayers, and so sanctified this place also.

12.6.0.en: Abram continued his journeying with his tent toward the south of Palestine, and in every place he went to he pitched his tent and built an altar. These are the two clear marks in Abram's life throughout his days: the tent and the altar, that is, being a stranger to the world and loving God.

12.7.0.en: The land of Canaan depended largely on rain for agriculture, so it seems that the rains had diminished, the crops were affected and a famine occurred. Abram did not think of returning to Mesopotamia, his original country, because God had commanded him to leave it, but he thought of going to Egypt, known for its wealth and abundant crops because of the Nile River in it; yet he did not wait for guidance from God to go there. Here Abram's weakness appears, in that he could not bear the distress of hunger, although it is not said of it that it was a severe famine as the Scripture says of the days of Jacob (ch. 43:1) or of the days of Joseph (ch. 47:20), and despite his knowing that the Egyptians were sensual and wicked, since he feared that they would kill him and take from him his beautiful wife Sarah. That is, he went to evil by himself, and his heart was tormented when they took his wife from him.

12.7.1.en: Endure the afflictions that come upon you and ask for God's help, and He will support you. Do not be troubled and rush into actions that take you away from God, or rely on crooked ways to save yourself, lest you fall into many troubles.

12.8.0.en: Abram continued in his weakness. While he was traveling on his way to Egypt, with Sarai his wife, Lot his nephew and Lot's wife, and his servants, he feared the wicked Egyptians when they would see his beautiful wife Sarai, even though her age at that time was nearing seventy, or at least beyond sixty-five; but because of their immersion in lust they could take her from him and kill him. So he said to her, "Say you are my sister" so that they would not kill him. Although she was his sister from his father, that is, not his full sister (ch. 20:12), the error here is clear: he lies, because he wants to deny that she is his wife so that they would not kill him. This is not only the sin of lying but also selfishness, since he thought of preserving his own life and did not think of Sarai, whom the Egyptians would take and do with her as they pleased; and it is also the sin of giving up his manhood and chivalry, since he was ready for his wife to be taken from him and married to another, without showing zeal to protect her.

12.9.0.en: It appears here that Sarai's beauty was very great, so that all the Egyptians admired her, and the news reached the king's palace, and the princes, the counselors of Pharaoh, praised her, so they took her to his palace to join his wives.

12.10.0.en: Pharaoh admired her beauty and rejoiced in her as a wife for himself, and offered her brother Abram a large bridal gift, as is customary from any bridegroom toward the family of his bride; and because this was the king himself, he gave many animals to Abram, knowing that his work was herding.

12.11.0.en: When God saw Abram's inability to defend himself, and saw also his spiritual weakness, He made allowance for him out of His fatherhood, because Abram was the only man in the world who worshipped God. For the sake of his faith He covered for him and intervened by striking Pharaoh and all who were with him with severe diseases, and then informed him that this was because he had taken Abram's wife. This divine intervention was swift, before he touched Sarai, so that Abram would not be tormented all his life because of his weakness and negligence ... It is the divine tenderness that surpasses all understanding.

12.12.0.en: Pharaoh was greatly afraid of Abram's God, who had struck and rebuked him, and he respected Abram very much. So he hurried to summon him and reproached him for not making clear that Sarai was his wife, and asked him to take his wife and leave Egypt, because he was afraid of him on account of the power of his God.

12.13.0.en: Pharaoh did not take back the gifts he had given Abram as a bridal gift for Sarai, and took care to send his servants to see him off with great honor as he returned from Egypt to Canaan. Thus God spoke with Abram by means of Pharaoh, who sent him back to Canaan, where God had commanded him to live. Yet when Abram obeyed God in simplicity, God used to speak to him directly and not through people; but in any case it shows the love of God, who brings His children back to life with Him however much they fall on the way and go far from Him.

12.13.1.en: The separation of Lot from Abram

13.0.0.en: So he went up: because Canaan lies north of Egypt.

13.0.1.en: Abram and all who were with him returned from Egypt to the south of Canaan, where he had been living before he went to Egypt.

13.1.0.en: Although Abram had erred, God covered for him and rescued him and restored Sarai to him, and even made him ashamed by the abundance of Pharaoh's gifts, in addition to God's blessing first upon his flocks, so that he became very rich in the animals he owned, and he even had much silver and gold, because he believed in God and accepted to leave his family and kindred to dwell in the wilderness.

13.1.1.en: In proportion to your faith, your reliance on God and your obedience to His commandments, however difficult they may seem, He will bless you with spiritual and material blessings, until you are ashamed at the abundance of His love, and He confirms your faith and your obedience to Him increases.

13.2.0.en: Abram moved north in the land of Canaan, shifting his tent from place to place until he reached Bethel, where he had been living (map 6). Thus he returned to the same place. Although he had needlessly wasted a time of his life by going down to Egypt and being exposed to a hard trial, he benefited from it and learned that his life is settled only in the wilderness, that is, in detachment, and before God's altar, where he raises prayers and sacrifices and finds his rest.

13.2.1.en: Do not stay away from the altar and from partaking of the Holy Mysteries, for they are your life. On the altar you lay all your requests, so you receive your strength, rise from your sins, enjoy fellowship with God and keep your peace in the midst of the world's turmoil.

13.3.0.en: God blessed the sheep and possessions of Lot as He blessed the possessions of Abram, because he believed in God and accompanied his uncle on the path of faith, detachment and renunciation for God's sake.

13.4.0.en: Because of the abundance of livestock, the pastures and springs of water became less than their needs, and each party of herdsmen tried to seize the better pastures when they went out each day to graze together, so clashes and troubles occurred between them. At the same time the tribes of the Canaanites and the Perizzites lived around them, and their herdsmen also went out with their livestock to graze, so it was an ugly sight, namely the quarreling and strife of believers, that is, Abram's herdsmen and Lot's herdsmen, before the pagans who inhabited the land.

13.5.0.en: Abram intervened when he heard of these quarrels and disputes among the herdsmen, and spoke with Lot to stop them. He addressed him with all humility, saying to him, "We are brethren," although Abram was the elder and his uncle, and he gave him the right to choose the land and the better pastures. He said to him, let us live together but separate a little, so that each one has the opportunity to graze freely, and let us stop the troubles so as to keep our peace and our love.

13.5.1.en: Here appears the importance of the spiritual leader, the head of the family or the servant in keeping peace for those with him and in solving problems.

13.5.2.en: Care for your peace above every other concern, whatever the cost, and humble yourself before all, give up any material thing and bear the offenses of those around you, for by this peace of yours you can continue your spiritual life, live in joy and win the love of many, and consequently be able to influence them and draw them to God.

13.6.0.en: The plain of Jordan: that is, the Jordan plain or the Jordan valley beside the river.

13.6.1.en: Well watered: water is abundant in it, whether from the Jordan River or from the pools that were abundant there. Sodom and Gomorrah: two cities lying south of the Dead Sea.

13.6.2.en: Zoar: a small city at the edge of the Jordan valley, southeast of the Dead Sea; it will also be discussed in (ch. 19). It seems that Lot went up on a hill and began to look for the most fertile place, or through his wandering in the land of Canaan and what he heard from its inhabitants, he learned that the plain of Jordan was a fertile land in which pastures and water were abundant, resembling in its fertility and wealth the land of Egypt, and he even likens it to the garden in which Adam and Eve lived, because of its great fertility. This plain includes the country of Sodom and Gomorrah and other lands; so he rejoiced in it and chose it to live in. Here appears Lot's material outlook, which troubled him greatly: although he believed in God, the love of material things blinded his eyes, so that he chose wealth rather than nearness to his uncle Abram, the leader of the path of faith. He could have moved a little way off so that no quarrels would occur between the herdsmen, and at the same time stayed in a close relationship with him to be taught at his hands, but he preferred material things over the spiritual life with Abram.

13.6.3.en: Beware of the love of money, for it is the root of all evils, and use everything in the world in moderation, and do not be immersed in its lusts, so that you give your faith the chance to grow and your love toward God to increase, and so you find the salvation of your soul.

13.7.0.en: Abram remained in the wilderness of Canaan, where there is detachment and being a stranger to the world, while Lot dwelt in Sodom, where the land was fertile, although he knew that the people of Sodom were wicked. But he made light of it and lived among the wicked, so his heart was tormented every day by what he saw of their evils, and even he and his family were influenced by them. It is the love of money that blinds a person from seeing God, so that he is lenient with evil.

13.8.0.en: God appeared a fourth time to Abram because he had returned to the life of detachment in the wilderness and let God choose for him the place where he would live, whereas Lot chose for himself material wealth. Thus Abram, the detached one, enjoyed seeing God many times, and even received great promises from Him, for He said to him, "Arise, walk" in the four directions, to declare to him that all the land in which he lived He would give to him and to his seed. Abram believed this although he had not yet been given offspring. His walking in the four directions is in the likeness of the cross, through which we receive all spiritual good things. And God's saying that He gives the land to Abraham's seed forever means by it throughout life on the earth, if they live in the same faith as Abram; but when they abandoned the faith they lost the land, as happened in the captivity and when they refused to believe in Christ, so Jerusalem was destroyed.

13.9.0.en: God promised him abundant offspring, which He likened to the dust of the earth, which cannot be counted because of its multitude, and then He asked him to walk through the land, confident that it had become his possession by God's promise.

13.10.0.en: Mamre: the name of an Amorite man.

13.10.1.en: Hebron: its meaning is companionship or union, and it is a village 20 miles south of Jerusalem, whose place is now the city of Hebron (al-Khalil), named after Abraham, the friend of God; it was first called Kirjath-arba, after a man named Arba, one of the chiefs of the tribe of the Anakim.

13.10.2.en: Abram rejoiced in God's promise and continued the life of a stranger, so he moved his tents to a region with some oak trees called the oaks of Mamre, beside a village called Hebron, and there he practiced his spiritual life by building an altar on which he offered many sacrifices and prayers (map 6).

13.10.3.en: When you read the Holy Bible and see the many promises of God offered to you, hold fast to your prayers and your estrangement from the world, so that God's blessings to you increase and God appears in your life and you enjoy Him.

13.10.4.en: Abram rescues Lot and meets Melchizedek
